extracted.intended_audience: Residents of Empress & District (local community readers, farmers, parents, consumers)
extracted.subtask_description: A single page of a 1928 local newspaper containing news items, editorial/commentary, practical advice for farmers and parents, product advertisements, and short how-to lists intended for a rural Canadian readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Go Broke — Rule 1: Grow only one crop
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of a satirical ten-rule list from the University of Tennessee extension titled “How to Go Broke Farming”; presented as contrarian advice showing what not to do if you want a prosperous farm.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Go Broke — Rule 2: Keep no livestock
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as one of ten intentionally bad rules to illustrate poor farm practice (no diversification or animal income).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Go Broke — Rule 3: Regard chickens and a garden as nuisances
rubrics_metrics.description: Regard chickens and a garden as nuisances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical admonition included in the ten rules illustrating neglect of small-scale productive activities that normally supplement farm income and subsistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Go Broke — Rule 4: Take everything from the soil and return nothing
rubrics_metrics.description: Take everything from the soil and return nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice to deplete soil fertility; listed to illustrate the anti-pattern of failing to practice soil conservation or crop rotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Go Broke — Rule 5: Don't stop gullies or grow topsoil; let crops wash away
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't stop gullies or grow topsoil; let the crops wash away, then you will have bottom land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical rule highlighting erosion and failure to conserve topsoil as a guaranteed path to ruin; warns implicitly that soil conservation is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Go Broke — Rule 6: Don't plan your farm operations; trust to luck
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't plan your farm operations; it's hard work thinking—trust to luck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the ten rules showing that lack of planning and management is a recipe for failure; implies that careful planning is required for success.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Go Broke — Rule 7: Regard woodland as a coal mine; cut every tree
rubrics_metrics.description: Regard your woodland as you would a coal mine — cut every tree, sell the timber and wear the cleared land out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical warning against short-term exploitation of woodland and failure to practice sustainable forestry or land management.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Go Broke — Rule 8: Hold fast to your grandfather's methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Hold fast to the idea that the methods employed by your grandfather are good enough for you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the ten anti-rules illustrating the danger of refusing to adopt improved methods or innovations in farming.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Go Broke — Rule 9: Be independent — don't join in co‑operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Be independent—don't join with your neighbors in any form of co-operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the ten-rule satire showing that rejecting cooperative action (marketing, purchasing, mutual aid) isolates producers and harms economic prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Go Broke — Rule 10: Mortgage your farm for every dollar it will stand
rubrics_metrics.description: Mortgage your farm for every dollar it will stand to buy things you would have the cash to buy if you followed a good system of farming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final satirical rule warning against excessive debt and poor financial management; implies prudent borrowing and investment are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infant fluid requirement guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: During the first six months, babies must have three ounces of fluid per pound of body weight daily; later the rule is two ounces per pound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice from a pediatric authority: example — an eight pound baby needs 24 ounces daily in first six months. For breast-fed infants, determine intake by weighing before and after feeding for the whole day; for bottle-fed infants calculate intake and make up any deficiency with water. Notes that adequate water can relieve feverishness, crying, upset, and restless spells; gives practical steps and cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rickets effects on teeth (childhood disease affecting tooth structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rickets: a disease of faulty nutrition that can cause deciduous teeth to erupt late, general deformity of skull and jaws, early loss of deciduous teeth, permanent teeth erupting late causing malocclusion; teeth may be structurally affected (bluish, sparse, tapering).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that teeth are formed in early childhood and are susceptible to systemic diseases; notes rickets occurs in both poor (insufficient food) and rich (improper diet) families; indicates clinical signs and long-term dental consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tuberculosis effects on teeth (childhood disease affecting tooth eruption)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tuberculosis: tends to cause early eruption of both deciduous and permanent teeth; the root of the deciduous tooth may not be absorbed properly, resulting in malposition of succeeding permanent teeth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides clinical explanation linking tuberculosis in childhood to disturbances of tooth eruption and consequent malocclusion; emphasizes timing of formative stages makes teeth vulnerable to systemic disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why Gum‑Dipping Increases Tire Life
rubrics_metrics.description: Gum-dipping puts a coating of new live rubber around each separate cord that keeps it from rubbing against adjacent cords, reducing friction and heat so the tire stays cooler and lasts longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ad explanation describing mechanical rationale: movement bends tire generating friction and heat that deteriorate tires; insulating each cord prevents cord-on-cord friction and heat buildup, improving durability and miles per dollar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tea quality assurance (Red Rose Orange Pekoe Tea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exacting cup tests carried out in blending rooms insure for Red Rose Orange Pekoe Tea a quality that is absolutely uniform; packed in aluminum to preserve peak freshness and flavor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising claim describing quality-control practice (cup tests in blending rooms) and packaging choice (aluminum) as means to guarantee uniformity and freshness; presented as assurances consumers can use to assess product quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of good permanent building paper (Hercules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Building paper should be tough, not tear easily, be windproof and dampproof, easy to use, and avoid cracking in use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ad copy arguing carpenters prefer a durable building paper that withstands rough handling and speeds construction; mentions product comes in three grades (x, xx, xxx) and offers samples — practical selection criteria for builders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons to support the Wheat Pool (producer co‑operation case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerated reasons urging wheat producers to support the Wheat Pool: self-protection is incomplete without collective action; cooperation suppresses exploitative middle-men and dividend-hunting shareholders; co-operation upholds grain quality standards; cooperative organization promotes economic and social justice; pooling resources counters hostile capitalistic organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persuasive list targeted at producers explaining the economic and social rationales for joining the Wheat Pool; presented as concrete benefits (price stability, standard maintenance, elimination of middlemen, collective bargaining power) and ideological justification.
